title: How to list PPE certifications and standards on product pages
summary: List each PPE certification as structured fields: the standard with its edition year, the exact rating earned, and the approval ID, verified against the source.
body_markdown:
List each PPE certification as structured attributes rather than a line of marketing copy: the standard with its edition year (` ANSI Z89.1-2009` ), the exact rating the product earned (` Type II` ,` Class E` ), and, where one exists, the approval or certificate ID, all shown as filterable spec fields with the test report or approval document attached. For respirators, publish the NIOSH TC approval number exactly as printed on the product and confirm it against NIOSH's Certified Equipment List before the page goes live.


That is the whole answer in two sentences. The rest of this post is the detail that makes it work in a catalog of thousands of SKUs: which standards apply to which PPE category, how to model them as fields, how to verify them, and why getting one wrong is a liability rather than a typo.


## What a PPE certification claim on a product page has to contain


A usable certification claim has four parts. Many product pages carry only one of them.


1. **The standard and edition.**` ANSI Z87.1` alone is incomplete. OSHA's eye and face rule,[29 CFR 1910.133](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.133) , names specific editions (` ANSI/ISEA Z87.1-2010` ,` Z87.1-2003` ,` Z87.1-1989 (R-1998)` ), so the edition is part of the compliance answer.
2. **The rating level.** "Cut resistant" tells a buyer nothing.` ANSI/ISEA 105 cut level A6` does.
3. **The certifier or approval ID.** A NIOSH TC number, a certification body's listing, or for the EU, the conformity documentation.
4. **The evidence.** The spec sheet, test report, EU declaration of conformity, or approval record the value came from.


Wording matters too. ISEA's[tips for buying PPE online](https://safetyequipment.org/tips-for-buying-ppe-amp-safety-equipment-online/) flags phrases like "ANSI certified", "ANSI approved" and "OSHA approved" as signs a seller may not understand the standards. ANSI publishes consensus standards and OSHA sets workplace rules; neither approves a specific product. Write "meets` ANSI Z89.1-2009` Type I, Class E" instead.


## Which PPE standards to list, by category


The standard that matters depends on the category. This table covers the common US categories plus the EU route, with the rating field each one needs.


PPE category Standard to cite Rating attribute to capture


Eye and face` ANSI/ISEA Z87.1` (edition per[1910.133](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.133) ) Standard edition, manufacturer marking


Head` ANSI/ISEA Z89.1` (editions per[1910.135](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.135) )` Type I` or` Type II` ,` Class G` ,` E` or` C`


Hand` ANSI/ISEA 105` ;` EN 388` for EU Cut` A1` -` A9` , abrasion` 0` -` 6` , puncture


Respiratory NIOSH approval TC number, filter class such as` N95` or` P100`


Foot` ASTM F2413` (2005 edition named in[1910.136](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.136) ) Protection claims from the standard


High-visibility` ANSI/ISEA 107`` Type O` ,` R` or` P` ,` Class 1` ,` 2` or` 3`


Flame-resistant` NFPA 2112` Certifier mark, standard edition


Any PPE sold in the EU Regulation (EU) 2016/425, CE Risk category, harmonised EN standard


A few notes on the fields behind that table, all from the sources linked.


**Hard hats.** Under Z89.1, a Type I helmet reduces impact from a blow to the top of the head and a Type II from the top or sides; Class G is proof-tested at 2,200 volts and Class E at 20,000 volts, while Class C offers no electrical protection, as[PK Safety's breakdown](https://pksafety.com/blogs/pk-safety-blog/types-classes-of-helmets-hard-hats) explains. Those are two separate attributes,` impact_type` and` electrical_class` , because buyers filter on each.


**Gloves.**[Intertek's ANSI/ISEA 105 summary](https://www.intertek.com/etl/standards/lss-ansi-isea-105/) lists cut on an` A1` -` A9` scale, abrasion on` 0` -` 6` , puncture and needle resistance in newtons, plus chemical and thermal properties. EN 388 rates abrasion, cut, tear and puncture with its own scheme, and[Ergodyne notes](https://www.ergodyne.com/blog/ansi-105-en-388-what-you-need-to-know) the two are not interchangeable. Store` ansi_cut_level` and` en388_code` as separate fields; never convert one into the other.


**Hi-vis.**[PSA Wear's ANSI/ISEA 107 guide](https://psawear.com/ansi-isea-107-hi-vis-class-guide/) describes Type O for off-road work, Type R for roadway exposure and Type P for public safety, with Classes 1 to 3, and points buyers to the sewn-in label, which states standard, type and class. Your page should match that label field for field.


**FR clothing.**[ISHN's NFPA 2112 explainer](https://www.ishn.com/articles/104526-what-you-should-know-about-nfpa-2112) describes the standard as covering performance of flame-resistant fabrics plus design and certification of garments for flash-fire areas, with the certification label attached to or positioned next to the FR clothing label. Capture who certified it, not only that it complies.


**EU sales.**[Regulation (EU) 2016/425](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/425/oj) has applied since 21 April 2018.[EU-OSHA's summary](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directive/regulation-eu-2016425-personal-protective-equipment) notes it sorts PPE into three risk categories with different conformity assessment procedures and requires an EU declaration of conformity. A CE mark field without the risk category and the EN standard behind it is a logo, not data.


Requirements and editions change. Treat the table as a starting map and confirm each standard's current edition with the manufacturer's documentation and the standard body before publishing.


## How to model PPE certifications as filterable attributes


The common failure is a single` certifications` text field holding "ANSI Z87.1, CSA, CE, meets OSHA". Nothing in it can be filtered, compared or validated. Break it into typed[product attributes](https://www.anglera.com/glossary/product-attributes) :


- ` standard_code` : controlled list, for example` ANSI/ISEA Z87.1`
- ` standard_edition` : year, for example` 2010`
- ` rating_value` : controlled per standard, for example` A6` ,` Type II` ,` Class 3`
- ` certifier_or_approval_id` : for example` TC-84A-xxxx` or the certification body
- ` evidence_document` : link to the spec sheet, test report or declaration
- ` verified_on` : the date someone checked the approval record


Most PPE needs several rows of this, one per standard. A cut-resistant, hi-vis glove carries both an ANSI/ISEA 105 row and, if sold in Europe, an EN 388 row.


For a fuller field list by category, see[the PPE attribute guide](https://www.anglera.com/blog/safety-ppe-attributes) .


## Verifying NIOSH approval on the Certified Equipment List


Respirators are where structured data and verification matter most. OSHA's respiratory protection standard,[1910.134(d)(1)(ii)](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.134) , says the employer "shall select a NIOSH-certified respirator", so your buyer's compliance depends on your data being right.


NIOSH's guide on[how to tell if an N95 is NIOSH approved](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2021-124/pdfs/2021-124.pdf) lists what the label on the respirator must show: the approval holder, part number, filter series and efficiency, the TC approval number such as` TC-84A-XXXX` , and "NIOSH" in capital block letters. It also says that if a TC number search on the[Certified Equipment List](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/NIOSH-CEL/) returns no results, the number is not a valid approval. The CEL also searches by manufacturer, protection type and private label, which matters because a distributor-branded respirator can carry another company's approval.


The practical check: for every respirator SKU, match both the model name and the TC number to the CEL, as NIOSH's[counterfeit and misrepresented respirators page](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/ppe/counterfeit_respirators/index.html) instructs. Record` verified_on` , and re-check on a schedule, because the CEL is the current record and your catalog is a copy of it.


## Why a wrong certification claim is a liability


A wrong claim does not sit quietly on a page. It flows into quotes, punchout catalogs and the customer's own safety records.


NIOSH distinguishes counterfeits (made to look like an approved model) from misrepresentation (products falsely marketed as NIOSH Approved). Its[published examples](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/ppe/counterfeit_respirators/ffr.html) include a company listing NIOSH on a technical specifications sheet without being an approval holder or private label assignee. A distributor that copies that spec sheet into its catalog republishes the false claim under its own name.


The same applies elsewhere. A glove listed as` A6` that tested` A4` , or a hard hat listed` Class E` that is vented` Class C` , puts the wrong product on a job where the buyer relied on your filter. Structured fields with evidence links make these errors findable; free text hides them.


## Where GS1 and syndication fit for PPE product data


GS1's[GDSN](https://www.anglera.com/glossary/gdsn-global-data-synchronization-network) carries certification marks too. GS1 Italy's[guide to certification-mark attributes](https://gs1it.org/content/public/64/95/6495266f-e541-443f-9e6c-be473cc04544/eng_gs1_guida_marchi_e_loghi_di_certificazione_v11_2023.pdf) describes` PackagingMarkedLabelAccreditationCode` , which records a third-party certification symbol printed on packaging. That tells a recipient a mark is present; it does not carry the cut level, hard hat class or TC number. Keep the rating attributes in your own model and map them to whatever fields each data pool or customer accepts, confirming against their current spec.


## Who does the extraction and upkeep


The work is reading the spec sheet, the approval record and the garment label, pulling the exact values into typed fields, and re-checking them when an approval changes. That is the work Anglera does: it extracts certification values from source documents, scores each one, flags conflicts (a spec sheet that says` A5` against a packaging image that says` A4` ) for review, and writes into your existing PIM or ERP, or a flat file. See[how it works](https://www.anglera.com/how-it-works) .


Your PIM stores the certification fields; someone still has to fill them from evidence and keep them current. If you run a safety catalog, the[safety and PPE distributor page](https://www.anglera.com/solutions/safety-ppe-distributors) shows how Anglera handles this alongside the PIM you already have, typically live within 30 days from a CSV or ERP export.
